title: Financial Leverage
subtitle: Amplifying profit - and risk
openingQuestion: Company A uses 50% debt, B uses 0% debt. Same 1 billion in assets, EBIT of 200 million. Whose ROE is higher?
openingOptions: A, because leverage amplifies ROE for shareholders
explanation: Financial leverage works through a single mechanism: debt has a fixed cost, so every unit of profit above that cost belongs entirely to shareholders - less equity, roughly the same profit, and ROE jumps. But that same mechanism runs in reverse just as sharply when ROIC falls below the borrowing rate, and interest still has to be paid on time regardless. So the real question when using leverage is how stable the cash flow is, not how attractive the ROE looks.

diagram.label: Replace part of equity with debt
Interest is a fixed cost, paid first
Profit above the interest cost flows entirely to shareholders
Above the borrowing rate ROE rises, below it ROE falls faster

realWorldExample.description: Many real estate businesses used high financial leverage to achieve impressive ROE during the favorable market period, but when the market turned, that same leverage caused ROE to collapse quickly, and some businesses fell into serious liquidity crises - clear proof of the two-edged nature of financial leverage.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk of high leverage?
options: When revenue falls, the fixed interest cost amplifies losses - financial distress
Shareholders resent having to share profit with creditors
Tax owed rises as interest makes profit more volatile
Profit ends up lower than an unlevered company under absolutely every possible scenario
quiz.explanation: Operating leverage + Financial leverage = Total leverage. When revenue falls 20%, a highly leveraged business could see EBIT fall 60-80%.

quiz.question: If a business's ROIC (return on invested capital) falls BELOW its cost of debt, how does financial leverage affect ROE compared to when ROIC was still above the cost of debt?
options: Leverage has no effect on ROE in this situation
It amplifies in the opposite direction - ROE falls more sharply than an unlevered company
ROIC has no bearing on how leverage affects ROE
Leverage always amplifies ROE upward no matter what ROIC turns out to be
quiz.explanation: This is the 'double-edged sword' of leverage: when ROIC > cost of debt, leverage amplifies ROE upward; but when ROIC < cost of debt, it amplifies in the opposite direction.

quiz.question: When does leverage increase ROE?
options: When the debt-to-equity ratio exceeds 1.0x
When revenue grows faster than fixed costs
When ROIC is higher than the after-tax cost of debt
When the market interest rate falls below inflation
quiz.explanation: Borrowing at 6% to generate a 12% return on invested capital means the 6% spread belongs to shareholders, and more borrowing amplifies it further. Reversed, a negative spread amplifies exactly the same way.

quiz.question: EBIT falls 20% at a highly leveraged company. How does net income change?
options: Unchanged, because interest was already deducted before EBIT
Falls exactly 20%, proportional to the EBIT decline
Falls less than 20%, because the tax shield offsets part of it
Falls more than 20%, because interest is a fixed cost
quiz.explanation: Interest doesn't fall with revenue. EBIT of 200 minus 30 interest leaves 170; if EBIT drops to 160, only 130 remains - a 24% drop, not 20%. Leverage amplifies in both directions.

quiz.question: Why should an industry with highly volatile revenue borrow less?
options: Because the fixed obligation to pay interest doesn't move while cash flow does
Because banks won't grant long-term loans to industries with volatile revenue
Because the tax rate applied to volatile industries is usually lower
Because leverage only works for steadily growing businesses
quiz.explanation: Debt capacity depends on how certain the cash flow used to service it is, not its average level. A single bad year in a cyclical industry can be enough to trip a covenant breach.

keyTakeaways: Leverage amplifies both profit and risk
ROIC > Kd: leverage helps; ROIC < Kd: leverage destroys value
Highly volatile industries should use less debt

practicePrompt.question: Two companies both invest 1,000 billion in a project, with an expected ROA of 12%. Company A funds it with 100% equity; company B funds it with 50% equity and 50% debt at an 8% interest rate. If the project succeeds as expected, which company has the higher ROE, and what happens if the project fails (ROA turns negative)?
options: B has the higher ROE when the project works (ROA 12% > 8% interest), but it also loses far more heavily if it fails
Company A always has a higher ROE than B in every scenario because it doesn't have to share profit with creditors
Both companies have the same ROE regardless of success or failure because they invested the same amount
Financial leverage only affects risk when the company fails, it has no effect at all when the company succeeds
practicePrompt.explanation: Leverage amplifies both profit and risk: when ROA (12%) > the borrowing rate (8%), using debt makes B's ROE higher than A's (a positive spread). But if the project fails and ROA turns negative, B still has to pay the fixed interest cost while having less equity to absorb the loss - making B's ROE fall far more sharply than A's.

summary.keyIdea: Leverage amplifies both profit and risk
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: ROIC > Kd: leverage helps; ROIC < Kd: leverage destroys value

application.title: Calculate ROE yourself under different leverage levels
application.message: Assume two scenarios for the same company - one using more debt, one using less - and calculate the ROE for both to see how leverage amplifies profit (and risk).
application.secondary: Try lowering the ROIC assumption below the cost of debt to see how leverage can backfire.

sections.text: Financial Leverage is Corporate Finance's classic double-edged sword: it amplifies return on equity (ROE) when everything goes well, but amplifies losses at the exact same rate when things turn bad.

Compare company A using leverage (Equity = 500 million, borrows the rest to generate EBIT = 200 million, pays 30 million interest → EBT = 170 million, roughly 136 million after tax → ROE = 136/500 = 27.2%) with company B using no debt (Equity = 1 billion, similar after-tax profit around 160 million → ROE = 16%). Company A has a much higher ROE because it used less equity to generate similar profit - this is exactly the amplification mechanism of leverage when ROIC (return on invested capital) is higher than the cost of debt.
When leverage amplifies in the opposite direction

That mechanism only holds when ROIC > cost of debt (Kd). If ROIC falls below Kd - typically when business turns difficult and revenue declines - leverage amplifies in the opposite direction: ROE falls much more sharply than for an unlevered company, because the business still has to pay fixed interest while returns on invested capital aren't enough to cover it. When revenue falls 20%, a highly leveraged business can see EBIT fall 60-80% - this mechanism sits behind many corporate financial crises, the classic example being Lehman Brothers' collapse in 2008 with a D/E over 30x.

left.label: ROIC > Cost of debt
left.text: Leverage is a 'friend' - it amplifies ROE higher than an unlevered company, with every additional unit of borrowed debt generating profit beyond the cost of servicing it.

right.label: ROIC < Cost of debt
right.text: Leverage becomes an 'enemy' - amplifying losses, since the company still has to pay fixed interest while operating profit isn't enough to cover it, accelerating the risk of financial distress.

items: Total leverage = Operating leverage × Financial leverage
Industries with high revenue volatility (real estate, commodities) should use less debt than stable industries (utilities, consumer staples)
During a favorable market period, high leverage produces impressive ROE - but it's exactly the same reason for rapid collapse when the market turns

lines: Leverage doesn't create value - it only amplifies the value (or value destruction) already present in the core business.
